Marriage and family

Worship and practice · Fasting, almsgiving, and family

Marriage and family

5 sectionsNot completed
Notes

The published marriage prayers ask for unity, love, peace and a life shaped by God’s commandments. St. Chrysostom’s accompanying passage connects forgiveness with the weakening of anger and the growth of love toward others.[1][2]

What does the first marriage prayer ask for?[1]

The prayer associates marriage with a bond of love and recalls St. Isaac and Rebecca. It asks blessing and guidance in good works for the couple. Its language belongs to the existing marriage office rather than a new prayer composed for this resource.[1]

Read original passage

Prayer at Holy Matrimony

O eternal God, who hast brought into unity those who were sundered, and hast ordained for them an indissoluble bond of love; who didst bless Isaac and Rebecca, and didst make them heirs of thy promise: Bless also these thy servants, N. and N., guiding them unto every good work. For thou art a merciful God, who lovest mankind, and unto thee do we ascribe glory, to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now, and ever, and unto ages of ages.

What does concord mean in the marriage prayer?[1]

Concord means peace and harmony between the couple. The prayer connects marriage with Christ’s presence at Cana and asks for faithfulness and a long shared life. It expresses these themes within the source’s sacramental prayer.[1]

Read original passage

Prayer for concord

O Lord our God, who in thy saving providence didst vouchsafe by thy presence in Cana of Galilee to declare marriage honourable: Do thou, the same Lord, now also maintain in peace and concord thy servants, N. and N., whom it hath pleased thee to join together. Cause their marriage to be honourable. Preserve their bed blameless. Mercifully grant that they may live together in purity; and enable them to attain to a ripe old age, walking in thy commandments with a pure heart.

How does St. Chrysostom explain forgiveness?[2]

St. Chrysostom describes forgiveness as beneficial to the person who forgives as well as to the relationship. He connects it with gentleness, love and the restraint of anger. The short selection provides a theological explanation rather than a script for a particular family disagreement.[2]

Read original passage

Forgiveness

Since He might indeed, even without this, forgive thee all thine offenses; but He wills thee hereby also to receive a benefit; affording thee on all sides innumerable occasions of gentleness and love to man, casting out what is brutish in thee, and quenching wrath, and in all ways cementing thee to him who is thine own member.

The OCA Holy Synod’s marriage statement[3]

This link identifies a statement on marriage issued by the OCA Holy Synod. Its issuing body and document remain the authority for the statement’s actual content.[3]
